questions.question: Explain the occurrence and nutritional significance of trypsin inhibitors in pulses. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the occurrence and nutritional significance of trypsin inhibitors in
  • pulses. (Any 5 points 1 mark each)
  • • Present in red gram, Bengal gram, cowpea, double beans, soya bean, Lathyrus
  • sativus, and peas.
  • • Inhibit trypsin – decrease protein digestion.
  • • Reduce release of essential amino acids (especially methionine).
  • • Cause pancreatic enlargement and growth retardation (in animals).
  • • Heat labile.
  • • Destroyed by moist heat (pressure cooking).
  • • Autoclaving at 120°C (15–30 min) → complete inactivation.
  • • Stronger heat needed for soybean and kidney bean.

questions.solution_html:
• Describe the process of homogenisation and its effect on fat globules in milk.
  • (1 mark for each point)
  • • Homogenisation- the process of making stable emulsion of milk fat and milk serum.
  • • Warm milk passed through small aperture under high pressure and velocity.
  • • Large fat globules are broken into very small, uniform globules.
  • • The surface area of fat increases and gets evenly distributed.
  • • Prevents cream separation and improves texture, stability, and digestibility.

questions.question: Discuss the processing of pulses, including soaking, germination, fermentation, parching and extrusion. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Discuss the processing of pulses, including soaking, germination, fermentation,
  • parching and extrusion.
  • Soaking- (2 marks)
  • • Pulses with hard outer covering need soaking before cooking.
  • • Water enters through the hilum and causes swelling of cotyledons.
  • • Makes pulses tender and reduces cooking time.
  • • Moisture content increases from 10% to 60–70%.
  • • Reduces phytic acid and oligosaccharides.
  • • Salt solution soaking improves water absorption and loosens seed coat.
  • • Soda reduces cooking time, but causes loss of thiamine.
  • • Hard water delays cooking.
  • • Causes leaching of water-soluble nutrients.
  • • Soaking water can be used in cooking to reduce nutrient loss.
  • Germination- (2 marks)
  • • Pulses are soaked overnight, drained, and kept moist for sprouting.
  • • Requires moisture and warmth; occurs in 1–2 days.
  • • Green gram germinates faster; process is quicker in summer.
  • • Enzymes are activated during germination.
  • • Starch → sugars, proteins → simpler forms (improves digestibility).
  • • Reduces trypsin inhibitors and phytic acid.
  • • Increases vitamins (especially B-complex) and Vitamin C is synthesized.
  • • Improves availability of minerals like iron, calcium, and zinc.
  • • Reduces cooking time and makes seeds softer.
  • • Decreases flatulence.
  • • Improves taste, texture, and palatability.
  • Fermentation- (2 marks)
  • • Fermentation involves microbial action that breaks down pulse components.
  • • Increases digestibility by breakdown of proteins.
  • • Improves palatability and cooking quality.
  • • Enhances nutritive value of pulses.
  • • Improves availability of essential amino acids.
  • • Helps in elimination of toxic substances (e.g., in idli preparation).
  • • Improves overall protein quality.
  • • Common examples: idli and dosa.
  • Parching- (2 marks)
  • • Parching is a dry heat treatment used to improve acceptability of pulses.
  • • Common pulses: Bengal gram and peas.
  • • Grains are first sprinkled with a little water.
  • • Then mixed with preheated sand in a frying pan.
  • • Heated on open fire at 200–250°C for 2–3 minutes.
  • • Produces roasted, ready-to-eat products with good flavor.
  • • Improves palatability and digestibility.
  • Extrusion- (2 marks)
  • • Blends of cereals and legume flour are extruded at high temperature (140–
  • 200°C) high pressure and moisture content <20%.
  • • The product is cooked for a short time, (30 to 60 seconds), and the product is
  • forced out of the extruder through a variety of dies and dried on conveyor
  • belts.
